source.title: Silencing the Guardrails: Inference-Time Jailbreaking via Dynamic Contextual Representation Ablation
source.authors: Wen-Peng Xing; Moran Fang; Guangtai Wang; Chang-Ting Lin; Meng Han

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure and table content is flattened or garbled; only values that can be assigned from the text or layout are recorded.
record.tranche_reason: The paper builds CRA, an inference-time attack that dynamically attributes and masks refusal-related activations, drawing on the refusal-subspace finding. It reports CRA’s attack performance, not a test of the original difference-in-means direction or of attacks that suppress that specific direction.
record.gate_note: CRA’s results concern its own dynamic, gradient-attributed neuron masking, not the original static difference-in-means direction. The paper’s stated RRSR is the share of outputs without standard refusal prefixes in their initial tokens. Cited results and baseline values not produced by the study itself are excluded. Table 2’s suppression-strength results are included model by model; the paper does not state their prompt-set condition there.
record.test_reason: CRA is the authors' own attack. It masks individual hidden-state dimensions chosen per token by gradients of refusal-token log-likelihood. It never computes or ablates the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, and it does no weight edit. The paper cites Arditi et al. as the motivation but reports only CRA's attack success, RRSR and fluency against other jailbreak methods. Its statement that cross-model success 'validates' a shared refusal direction is asserted, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that dynamic inference-time masking of refusal-related activations jailbreaks aligned 7B models efficiently and beats baselines. They also claim refusal is encoded in low-rank, early-layer subspaces separable from general reasoning. In addition, they assert that cross-model success shows models converge on a shared linear refusal representation. That last claim is interpretation, not a direct test.
record.recipe_differences: The original method derives a static refusal direction from harmful-minus-harmless mean activations and ablates that direction. CRA instead uses per-instance, per-token gradient attribution to select dimensions and dynamically masks them during decoding; it does not use the original difference-in-means direction.
record.method_sensitivity: CRA’s ASR-O varies with suppression strength λ and model: Table 2 reports a decline for Vicuna at λ=1.0 and increases for Llama-2 and Mistral. The paper also reports different Llama-2 ASRs for unrestricted, layer-restricted, and full CRA conditions. The text does not reconcile differing Llama-2 values across sections.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-attributed per-token neuron masking raises harmful-compliance ASR-O on Llama-2-7B-Chat from 36% (λ=0) to 64% (λ=1). It has little or negative effect on models that already comply at λ=0: Vicuna drops from 84% to 72%, while Guanaco and Mistral move about ±4 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic gradient-attributed masking of refusal-related activations increases harmful compliance in strongly aligned models, with effects depending on model and suppression strength.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama-2, full-strength CRA removes refusal prefixes in 96.3% of initial tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Full-strength CRA nearly eliminates refusal-prefix tokens on Llama-2-7B-Chat.

fits_no_version.finding: Targeted masking beats random masking at equal density (76% vs 40%). First-5-block masking slightly beats last-5 (42% vs 38%). Fluency proxies degrade as λ rises.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CRA's effectiveness depends on attribution targeting and layer range, at some fluency cost.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper does not test the original difference-in-means direction; there are inconsistencies or unreconciled Llama-2 ASR-O values across sections (53.0%, 64.0%, and 76.0%). The suppression-strength table does not state its prompt-set condition. Numerical uncertainty is not supplied for the tabulated ASRs, and the capability discussion uses Self-BLEU and N-gram diversity rather than a direct benign-task capability evaluation. Some table/figure text is flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for individual benchmark bars in Figure 4 or baseline results were extracted because the flattened chart text does not reliably assign every number to a model, method, and dataset. Figure-only strength-sweep values without explicit textual numbers were also omitted.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is computed. There is no ablation or addition of such a direction and no test of refusal induction. Only per-token gradient-selected neuron masking is used.
No weight orthogonalization or abliterated released model is evaluated.
No test of whether existing jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation.
No comparison of single-direction vs. multi-direction, cone or affine accounts. CRA's 'subspace' is a set of masked coordinates.
Harmfulness judgment and the refusal decision are not measured separately.
Each model's masks are computed independently, so nothing tests whether a direction transfers across languages, variants, or base vs. instruct models.
Refusal training method and timing are not varied. The Vicuna-vs-Llama-2 contrast is explained post hoc, not tested.

missing.what: Localization-strategy ablation: Sensitivity Only gives 52.0% ASR-O and Salience Only 55.0%, with corresponding RRSR and fluency values (CRA-internal, no version)
Per-dataset (PKU, ToxicChat, AdvBench) ASR-O for Direct, PEZ, ED and CRA across four models; figure text is garbled

record.verdict_notes: Llama-2 ASR-O values conflict across sections (53.0, 64.0, 76.0) without explanation. The λ=0 'CRA' results equal the unattacked behaviour. No difference-in-means direction is ever extracted, so nothing here bears on the claim's versions.

versions.untested_parts: Does not find a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction or apply that direction across every layer and position; CRA uses dynamic gradient attribution and masking.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is evaluated.
CRA is itself a dynamic activation-masking attack; the paper does not test whether other attacks suppress the claim’s single direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
Cross-model CRA results do not test transfer of one identified direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.

rows.note: Reported as the CRA suppression-strength sweep; the paper does not state the prompt-set condition for this table.
rows.check: At λ=0.0 no masking is applied (h̃=h). This is effectively the unattacked model under the CRA pipeline, so it is a baseline, not a CRA result. The same holds for r7, r13 and r19. These values show Vicuna (84%), Guanaco (80%) and Mistral (80%) already comply heavily without intervention.
